paragraphs.heading: The largest toothed whale
paragraphs.text: The sperm whale, also called the cachalot, is the biggest toothed whale and also the biggest predator with teeth. It is the only living member of its genus, Physeter. It is a mammal with a worldwide range, and it migrates with the seasons to feed and breed. Mature males average 16 metres long, and the head can make up as much as a third of that length.

paragraphs.heading: Deep, loud and long-lived
paragraphs.text: It dives to 2,250 metres, which makes it the third deepest diving mammal. Only the southern elephant seal and Cuvier's beaked whale go deeper. It uses echolocation and makes sounds as loud as 236 decibels underwater, the loudest of any animal. Its brain is the largest on Earth, more than five times as heavy as a human's. Sperm whales can live 70 years or more. A mature, healthy one has no natural predators, though pods of orcas sometimes kill calves and weakened adults.

paragraphs.heading: Family life
paragraphs.text: Females and young males live together in groups. Mature males, called bulls, live alone outside the mating season. The females work together to protect and nurse their young. A female gives birth every four to twenty years, and calves are cared for over more than a decade.

paragraphs.heading: Spermaceti and whaling
paragraphs.text: The whale's head is filled with a semi-liquid, waxy substance called spermaceti. The whaling industry made it a prime target, wanting it for oil lamps, lubricants and candles. In the 19th century sperm whaling was a major industry, and the novel Moby-Dick depicts it. Ambergris, a solid waxy waste sometimes present in the whale's digestive system, remains highly valued, with use as a fixative in perfumes. The International Whaling Commission moratorium protects the species, and the International Union for Conservation of Nature lists it as vulnerable.

paragraphs.heading: Where the names come from
paragraphs.text: "Sperm whale" is a shortened form of "spermaceti whale". Spermaceti was at first mistaken for the whale's semen. The other name, cachalot, is thought to come from an archaic French word for 'tooth' or 'big teeth'. The genus name Physeter comes from a Greek word meaning 'blowpipe' or 'blowhole'. The species name macrocephalus comes from the Greek for 'big-headed'.

paragraphs.heading: Two rival scientific names
paragraphs.text: Carl Linnaeus described the sperm whale in 1758, in the 10th edition of Systema Naturae. He recognised four species in the genus Physeter, but experts soon realised there is just one. That left a debate over which of two names Linnaeus used should stand, catodon or macrocephalus. Catodon means 'down-tooth', given because the whale has visible teeth only in its lower jaw. The species was generally known by the name catodon until 1974. Now most recent authors take macrocephalus to be the valid name.
